headline: Dutch Police Arrest Former Hacker Linked to Major Cybercrime Group

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Police in the Netherlands arrested a 23-year-old man named Pepijn van der Stap. Years ago, he broke computer rules by stealing private information from websites and selling it. He went to prison for this, but was let out a few months ago. He said he wanted to be a better person and got a new job helping companies stay safe from hackers. But police think he may have helped a hacker group called ShinyHunters do bad things again, so they arrested him and took things from his house. Right after he was arrested, ShinyHunters did something very bold: they broke into a website used by the FBI, which is like America's top detective agency, and stole private information about workers there. Experts think a teenager from another country may now be leading ShinyHunters and is fighting with Pepijn for control of the group. This story shows how tricky it can be to trust that someone has truly changed, and how much damage hackers can cause when they steal people's private information from big, important places.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: A 23-year-old Dutch man named Pepijn van der Stap was arrested again by police, even though he had already served time in prison for hacking crimes. Years earlier, he secretly stole private data from millions of people and sold it online while working a normal job during the day at a cybersecurity company. After getting out of prison, he told a reporter he had changed and wanted to help protect people from hackers instead. But police now suspect he secretly helped a hacking group called ShinyHunters, known for stealing data and demanding money to keep it secret. Right after his arrest, ShinyHunters attacked the FBI's job application website, stealing sensitive files about FBI employees, including some medical records. They also picked a fight with a Russian hacking group. Experts believe the real leader now controlling ShinyHunters is actually a teenager from Jordan who wanted to blame the attacks on Pepijn by using his old hacker symbol, a Pokémon character called Umbreon, as a clue. This case matters because it shows how hacking groups can hurt real people, steal sensitive personal information, and even target powerful government agencies like the FBI. It also raises hard questions about whether someone who did something wrong in the past can truly be trusted again, and how complicated online crime investigations can become when several hackers and countries are involved.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Dutch police recently arrested Pepijn van der Stap, a 23-year-old man who had already been convicted once for hacking crimes. Years before, using the online name 'Umbreon,' he broke into computer systems, stole personal data belonging to millions of people, and sold or leaked it while secretly living a double life as a legitimate software engineer. After serving part of a four-year prison sentence, he was released and told a reporter he wanted to change and use his skills to help companies defend against hackers instead. However, investigators suspect he may have kept helping a well-known hacking and extortion group called ShinyHunters, which steals sensitive data and threatens to release it unless victims pay money. Just days after his arrest, ShinyHunters carried out one of its boldest attacks yet: breaking into an FBI job application website and stealing sensitive records, including Social Security numbers and even psychiatric files of FBI employees. The hackers exploited a security weakness in widely used business software made by Oracle, a flaw that had already been patched but was still being exploited by attackers who found ways around companies' defenses. Interestingly, the hackers left behind digital 'graffiti' referencing Umbreon, van der Stap's old hacker alias, which some experts believe was intentional — an attempt by a rival hacker, allegedly a teenager from Jordan, to frame him or take credit for controlling the group. This event highlights several important real-world lessons: how difficult it is to verify whether someone who committed cybercrimes has truly reformed, how vulnerable even powerful institutions like the FBI can be to hackers, and how cybercriminal groups sometimes turn on each other when money and reputation are at stake. It also shows how a single unpatched security flaw in software used by many organizations can put thousands of people's private information at risk all at once.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Dutch authorities arrested 23-year-old Pepijn van der Stap earlier this month on suspicion of helping the hacking collective ShinyHunters carry out data thefts and extortion schemes. This is not van der Stap's first brush with the law: in 2023, he was convicted for using the hacker alias 'Umbreon' to steal and sell personal data belonging to millions of people, earning over a million euros while secretly working as a legitimate cybersecurity software engineer. After being released from prison in late 2025, he told a journalist he had reformed and taken a new job helping organizations defend against cyberattacks. Just weeks later, though, he stopped responding to messages, and sources say he was quietly arrested and questioned again, with police removing items from his home. Almost immediately after his detainment, ShinyHunters launched a highly public and aggressive campaign, breaching the FBI's job application website and stealing sensitive employee data, including Social Security numbers and confidential medical and psychiatric records. The attackers exploited a software vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft platform, a system many organizations use for human resources and payroll, even bypassing security defenses that had been put in place after the flaw was first discovered. Notably, the hackers included imagery referencing 'Umbreon' in their attack, which cybersecurity investigators believe may have been a deliberate move by a rival — reportedly a teenage hacker from Jordan known online as 'Rey' — to pin blame on van der Stap while seizing control of the ShinyHunters brand for himself. This apparent power struggle reflects a larger pattern in cybercrime: alliances between hacking groups often collapse into rivalries once large profits are involved, with some estimates suggesting ShinyHunters could earn close to $100 million in extortion payments this year alone. The situation also raises tough questions about rehabilitation — whether someone convicted of serious cybercrimes can genuinely change, and how authorities can tell the difference between reform and relapse. More broadly, the case underscores how a single overlooked or slowly patched software vulnerability can expose sensitive information from powerful institutions like the FBI, showing that even highly secure government systems are not immune to sophisticated, coordinated cyberattacks.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: The arrest of 23-year-old Pepijn van der Stap by Dutch police has reignited scrutiny of one of the most active and damaging hacking collectives currently operating: ShinyHunters. Van der Stap was previously convicted in 2023 for a string of data thefts and extortion schemes carried out under the alias 'Umbreon,' through which he stole and sold personal information belonging to millions of people while maintaining a parallel career as a legitimate cybersecurity professional. After serving part of his sentence, he was released in December 2025 and publicly presented himself as reformed, taking a position as an offensive security lead — someone paid to test and strengthen organizations' cyber defenses. Yet within weeks of that public rehabilitation narrative, he reportedly went silent and was arrested again on suspicion of continuing to assist ShinyHunters, with authorities removing materials from his residence. The timing is striking: almost immediately after his detainment, ShinyHunters escalated its operations dramatically, breaching the FBI's job application portal and extracting sensitive data on thousands of employees, including Social Security numbers, job assignments in sensitive units, and confidential psychiatric and medical files. The group exploited a vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software, a platform widely used for human resources and payroll functions, bypassing firewall protections that cybersecurity firms had recommended as a stopgap before an official patch could be fully deployed. This breach followed a broader pattern of aggressive exploitation across sectors including higher education, healthcare, and government. Adding a layer of intrigue, the digital defacement left on the FBI site prominently featured 'Umbreon' imagery, seemingly implicating van der Stap. However, investigators and outside sources suggest this was likely a deliberate misdirection orchestrated by a rival figure — a teenage hacker based in Jordan known as 'Rey,' who is believed to have seized control of the ShinyHunters brand as part of a broader alliance called ScatteredLapsussHunters, merging several notorious hacking groups. Reporting indicates that tensions between van der Stap and Rey stemmed from a fractured partnership with another hacking crew, TeamPCP, whose stolen credentials were secretly neutralized by cybersecurity researchers working with major cloud providers — leading the implicated hacker groups to turn on one another over lost profits. This saga illustrates several significant real-world dynamics: the fragile and often self-interested alliances that form within cybercriminal ecosystems, the immense financial incentives driving modern extortion operations (with ShinyHunters reportedly on pace to collect close to $100 million this year), and the profound difficulty of verifying genuine rehabilitation in individuals with deep technical expertise and prior criminal networks. It also spotlights systemic vulnerabilities in widely used enterprise software that, when exploited, can expose deeply sensitive personal and institutional data — even from an agency as security-conscious as the FBI — underscoring how interconnected and fragile digital infrastructure can be.

questions: If someone has served their punishment for breaking the law, how much trust do you think they should be given afterward, and what could help prove they've truly changed?

This story shows that even powerful organizations like the FBI can have their private information stolen. How do you think this affects how safe we should feel about our own personal data being stored online?
The hacking groups in this story eventually turned against each other over money and credit. What does this tell you about trust and teamwork, even among people working toward the same goal?
